name: Dexmethylphenidate (Focalin, Focalin XR)
summary: Stimulant for ADHD in people 6 and older. Improves focus and impulse control but can cause appetite loss, slowed growth in children, heart and mood effects, and has a high risk of abuse and addiction.
description: Dexmethylphenidate is the active half of methylphenidate, the stimulant used in many ADHD medications. It is sold as short acting Focalin tablets and long acting Focalin XR capsules. It boosts norepinephrine and dopamine in parts of the brain that control attention and self control. This can significantly improve ADHD symptoms in children, teens, and adults, but it can also cause decreased appetite, weight loss, trouble sleeping, anxiety, and increases in heart rate and blood pressure. Dexmethylphenidate is a Schedule II controlled substance with a boxed warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction. In July 2025, the FDA highlighted that extended release stimulants, including Focalin XR, cause higher blood levels and more side effects in children younger than 6, including significant weight loss. Extended release forms are not recommended in this age group.
patient_summary:
Dexmethylphenidate (Focalin and Focalin XR) is a stimulant medicine for ADHD. It helps people focus better, sit still longer, and think before acting. Focalin is short acting and usually taken twice a day. Focalin XR is long acting and taken once each morning.

Common side effects are decreased appetite, weight loss, stomach pain, headache, trouble sleeping, and feeling more anxious or irritable. The medicine can also raise heart rate and blood pressure, so doctors check vitals regularly. In kids, it can slow weight gain and sometimes height growth, so height and weight are tracked over time.

Dexmethylphenidate has a high risk of misuse and addiction and is a Schedule II controlled substance. It must be used exactly as prescribed, never shared, and stored securely. In July 2025, the FDA warned that long acting stimulants like Focalin XR can cause higher drug levels and more side effects, including at least ten percent weight loss, in children younger than 6. Long acting stimulants are not recommended for this age group.

Talk with your prescriber about the benefits and risks, especially for young children or if there is a history of heart disease, significant mental health conditions, or substance use problems.

linked_conditions.context: FDA approved for ADHD in children 6 and older, adolescents, and adults. Often used when methylphenidate is effective but a more potent, smaller dose is preferred.

contraindications: Allergy to methylphenidate, dexmethylphenidate, or any component of the product
Use of a monoamine oxidase inhibitor within the past 14 days
Known serious structural heart disease or serious heart rhythm problems where stimulants may increase risk, based on prescriber judgment

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Approximately 22 to 25 percent for the active enantiomer
pharmacokinetics.onset: About 1 to 2 hours for immediate benefit at an effective dose
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate release: about 1 to 1.5 hours; extended release: two peaks, around 1.5 and 6.5 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: About 2 to 3 hours in children and about 3 hours in adults
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: De esterification to an inactive metabolite (d ritalinic acid)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily in urine as inactive metabolite
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High fat meals may delay peak for immediate release and have minimal effect on overall exposure

sections.heading: What It Is Used For
sections.text: Dexmethylphenidate is a stimulant used to treat ADHD. It is generally not used for other conditions.
items: {link:condition:adhd:Attention Deficit or Hyperactivity Disorder}: Helps reduce inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity at home, school, or work.
Adult ADHD: Improves focus, organization, and productivity in adults diagnosed with ADHD.
Alternative when methylphenidate works but causes side effects at higher doses: Dexmethylphenidate is the more active half of methylphenidate and is usually given at about half the dose.

sections.heading: July 2025 FDA Safety Update: Extended Release Stimulants in Children Under 6
sections.text:
In July 2025, the FDA issued a safety communication about extended release stimulant medications, including Focalin XR and other amphetamine and methylphenidate based products, in children younger than 6 years.

In studies of extended release stimulants for ADHD, children under 6 had higher blood levels of the medicine than older children and higher rates of side effects, including weight loss of at least ten percent of body weight.

Because of these findings, the FDA now requires the prescribing information for all extended release stimulants to clearly state a limitation of use in children under 6. Extended release stimulants are not recommended in this age group.

For children younger than 6 who are taking an extended release stimulant and are losing weight or having other side effects, the FDA advises clinicians to consider stopping the medicine, switching to an immediate release stimulant or a non stimulant option, and closely monitoring growth and nutrition. Parents and caregivers should talk with the prescriber if their child is under 6 and taking an extended release stimulant or if they notice significant weight loss.

sections.heading: What People Often Notice
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but common patterns with dexmethylphenidate include:

quotes: It was easier to stay on one task instead of bouncing between five things.
I could listen in class without my mind wandering every minute.
I finally finished work that I had been putting off for weeks.
I did not feel so driven to move all the time.
I stopped blurting things out as much in meetings.
I could wait my turn in conversations and with my kids.
I was not hungry at lunch and lost a few pounds.
My child eats a big breakfast before the pill but barely wants lunch.
If we give it too late in the day, bedtime is really hard.
I felt a little more on edge at first.
On stressful days, it can make me feel wired instead of focused.
We had to lower the dose because my child got irritable in the evenings.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works and How Long It Lasts
sections.text: Dexmethylphenidate starts working within hours and the duration depends on whether it is the short acting or long acting form.
key_points: Immediate release (Focalin): onset in about 1 to 2 hours, effect lasts about 3 to 5 hours.
Extended release (Focalin XR): first peak about 1 to 2 hours after dosing, second peak around 6 to 7 hours, overall effect about 9 to 12 hours.
Because of its short half life, immediate release tablets are usually taken twice a day, while extended release capsules are usually taken once each morning.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Dexmethylphenidate has a boxed warning for abuse, misuse, and addiction and is a Schedule II controlled substance.
sections.black_box: Stimulants, including dexmethylphenidate, have a high potential for abuse and misuse. Misuse can lead to the development of a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse, especially at high doses or by snorting or injecting, can cause serious heart problems, overdose, and death. Clinicians must assess risk of misuse before prescribing, educate patients and families, monitor throughout treatment, and use the lowest effective dose.
other: Serious heart problems: Sudden death, stroke, and heart attack have been reported in people with underlying heart disease taking stimulants. Stimulants can increase heart rate and blood pressure.
Psychiatric effects: Stimulants can cause or worsen anxiety, irritability, aggression, or, rarely, psychotic or manic symptoms such as hallucinations or paranoia.
Growth suppression: In children and adolescents, long term use can slow weight gain and height growth. Regular monitoring is required.
Circulation problems: Some people develop Raynaud like symptoms in fingers or toes, with color changes, numbness, or pain.
Eye issues: Stimulants can raise eye pressure and may trigger acute angle closure glaucoma in susceptible people.
Use in children under 6: Not recommended for extended release forms because of higher exposure and side effect risk, including significant weight loss.
patient_counseling: Never share this medicine with anyone, even if they have similar symptoms.
Store it safely in a place that is locked or not easily found. It has street value and can be misused.
Tell your prescriber about any heart problems, fainting, chest pain, or family history of sudden cardiac death.
Report new or worsening mood changes, anxiety, agitation, or hallucinations right away.
Children on stimulants should have their height and weight checked regularly. If they are not growing as expected, talk to the prescriber.
If you notice pale, blue, or painful fingers or toes, let the prescriber know.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most side effects are related to appetite, sleep, mood, and heart rate. Some are mild and manageable; others are serious and need prompt medical attention.
plain_language_list: Decreased appetite and weight loss, especially around lunchtime or during the day.
Trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.
Feeling nervous, anxious, or more irritable.
Mild increases in heart rate and blood pressure.

common.incidence: Very common in children and teens; decreased appetite reported in about one third of pediatric patients.
common.patient_note: Kids may skip lunch or eat less during the school day, then feel hungrier in the evening. Growth charts should be checked regularly.

common.incidence: Very common in children, teens, and adults.
common.patient_note: Often worse when starting or increasing the dose. Staying hydrated and taking the medicine with food can help.

common.symptom: Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or indigestion
common.patient_note: Taking the dose after breakfast may reduce stomach upset. Strong or persistent stomach pain should be evaluated.

common.incidence: Common, especially if the dose is high or taken later in the day.
common.patient_note: Taking long acting doses early in the morning and avoiding afternoon doses can help. Good sleep habits are important.
Sipping water, chewing sugar free gum, and good dental hygiene can help.

common.symptom: Anxiety, jitteriness, irritability, or mood swings
common.incidence: Reported in a minority of patients but clinically important.
common.patient_note: Sometimes improves with dose reduction or a different formulation. If severe, call the prescriber.

serious: Chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting, or an unusually fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat.
New hallucinations, paranoia, or manic behavior.
Severe aggression or sudden extreme mood changes.
Signs of poor circulation in hands or feet, such as pain, color changes, or sores that do not heal.
Unexplained, significant weight loss or failure to grow in children.
Severe allergic reactions, including swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing.
Severe muscle pain, dark urine, or weakness, which can be signs of muscle breakdown.

sections.heading: Drug and Substance Interactions
sections.intro: Many medicines and substances can interact with dexmethylphenidate. Always tell your prescriber about everything you take, including over the counter medicines and supplements.

items.risk: Dangerous rise in blood pressure and other serious reactions.
items.action: Cannot be used together. At least 14 days should pass between stopping a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and starting dexmethylphenidate.

items.with: Other stimulants, including other ADHD medicines and high dose caffeine
items.risk: Higher risk of increased heart rate, blood pressure, anxiety, and insomnia.
items.action: Avoid overlapping stimulants unless specifically directed by a specialist. Limit energy drinks and high caffeine products.

items.risk: Stimulants can reduce the effect of some blood pressure medicines.
items.action: Blood pressure should be checked regularly. Prescribers may adjust doses.

items.risk: Possible additive effects on heart rhythm.
items.action: Use caution. Prescribers may avoid combinations or monitor with electrocardiograms and vital signs.

items.risk: Can worsen judgment, anxiety, and sleep problems. Some extended release formulations of stimulants can release faster with alcohol.
items.action: Best to avoid alcohol while taking dexmethylphenidate, especially in younger people.

sections.heading: Dosing Overview
sections.text: Exact dosing must be chosen and adjusted by a prescriber. The following is a simplified overview for education only.

adult.adhd_initial_ir: Often 2.5 milligrams by mouth twice daily, at least four hours apart.
adult.adhd_titration_ir: Increased by 2.5 to 5 milligrams per day at weekly intervals, based on effect and side effects.
adult.adhd_max_ir: Common upper limit is 20 milligrams per day, although some specialists may cautiously use higher doses with close monitoring.
adult.adhd_initial_xr: Often 10 milligrams by mouth once daily in the morning.
adult.adhd_titration_xr: Increased by 10 milligrams per day at weekly intervals.
adult.adhd_max_xr: Common upper limit is 40 milligrams per day in adults, though lower doses are often effective.
adult.simple_explanation: Immediate release is given in smaller doses twice a day and wears off sooner. Extended release is taken once daily in the morning and is designed to cover most of the day.

pediatric.adhd_initial_ir: Children 6 and older often start at 2.5 milligrams twice daily, at least four hours apart.
pediatric.adhd_titration_ir: Increased by 2.5 to 5 milligrams per day at weekly intervals.
pediatric.adhd_max_ir: Many children respond at or below 20 milligrams per day. Some may require higher doses under specialist care, with careful monitoring.
pediatric.adhd_initial_xr: Children 6 and older often start at 5 milligrams once daily in the morning.
pediatric.adhd_titration_xr: Increased by 5 milligrams per day at weekly intervals.
pediatric.adhd_max_xr: Many guidelines suggest a maximum of 30 milligrams per day in children, though higher doses may be used by specialists with close monitoring.
pediatric.limitation: Extended release formulations are not recommended for children younger than 6 years.

sections.heading: Special Populations
sections.text: Some groups require extra care when using dexmethylphenidate.
sections.pregnancy: Data on dexmethylphenidate are limited. Most information comes from methylphenidate as a class. Prescribers balance the risks of untreated ADHD, such as accidents or difficulty functioning, against possible medication risks. If used during pregnancy, the lowest effective dose is preferred and decisions should be made jointly with the patient.
sections.lactation: It is not known if dexmethylphenidate itself is present in human milk, but methylphenidate is found at low levels. Breastfed infants should be monitored for poor weight gain, irritability, or sleep problems. Decisions about breastfeeding while on stimulants should consider the benefits of breastfeeding, the benefits of treatment for the parent, and potential risks to the infant.
sections.pediatrics: Approved and commonly used in children 6 and older. Extended release forms are not recommended under age 6 due to higher exposure and increased side effects, including significant weight loss. Growth monitoring is essential.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults may be more sensitive to increases in blood pressure, heart rate, and appetite loss. Lower starting doses and slower titration are usually recommended, with close monitoring for heart and mood effects.
sections.hepatic: Dexmethylphenidate is metabolized in the liver, but clinically significant liver impairment has not been well studied. Prescribers often start at lower doses and titrate slowly if liver disease is present.
sections.renal: Very little active drug is excreted unchanged in the urine. Dose adjustment for kidney disease is not usually required, but overall health and comorbidities are considered.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Before starting: personal and family heart history, including sudden death or serious arrhythmias.
Baseline blood pressure and heart rate.
Baseline weight and height in children and adolescents.
Screening for tics, Tourette syndrome, mood disorders, psychosis, and substance use problems.
During treatment: blood pressure and heart rate after dose changes and periodically.
Weight and height in children and teens, tracked over time on growth charts.
Weight in adults, especially if appetite is significantly reduced.
Mood and behavior changes, including anxiety, agitation, aggression, or hallucinations.
Signs of misuse or diversion, such as early refill requests, lost prescriptions, or doses taken differently than prescribed.
Signs of circulation problems in fingers and toes.
Eye symptoms in people with glaucoma or at risk for glaucoma.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Dexmethylphenidate is available as short acting tablets and long acting capsules.
items: Extended release capsules (Focalin XR): 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, and 40 milligrams.
Immediate release tablets are usually taken twice a day. Extended release capsules are taken once each morning and must not be crushed or chewed.
Extended release capsules can be opened and the contents sprinkled on a small amount of applesauce and swallowed right away without chewing.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.text: Dexmethylphenidate is the more active d enantiomer of methylphenidate. It blocks the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine into nerve cells and increases their release into the space between cells. This raises the levels of these chemicals in brain regions that control attention, alertness, and impulse control. In people with ADHD, this usually leads to better focus and less hyperactive or impulsive behavior.

sections.heading: Place in ADHD Treatment
sections.text: Dexmethylphenidate is one of several first line stimulant options for ADHD. It is often chosen when methylphenidate is effective but a more potent, lower dose option is desired, or when once daily extended release coverage is preferred. It is usually used as part of a comprehensive ADHD treatment plan that may include behavioral strategies, school or workplace accommodations, parent training, and therapy. For preschool aged children, behavioral interventions are typically tried before medications, and extended release stimulants are not recommended under age 6.

seo.title: Dexmethylphenidate (Focalin, Focalin XR): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects, and 2025 FDA Safety Update
seo.description: Dexmethylphenidate for ADHD: how it works, immediate release vs extended release, typical dosing, side effects, abuse and addiction risk, growth and heart monitoring, and the 2025 FDA warning about extended release stimulants in children under 6.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content drafted from current prescribing information, FDA safety communications as of July 2025, and major professional guidelines on ADHD diagnosis and treatment.

faqs.a: Dexmethylphenidate is used to treat ADHD in children 6 and older, adolescents, and adults. It helps improve attention, reduce hyperactivity, and control impulsive behavior at school, work, and home.

faqs.q: How is Focalin different from Focalin XR
faqs.a: Focalin is the short acting tablet. It usually works for about 3 to 5 hours and is taken twice a day. Focalin XR is the long acting capsule. It is taken once each morning and can last 9 to 12 hours. Focalin XR must be swallowed whole or opened and sprinkled on applesauce, then swallowed without chewing.

faqs.q: How long does dexmethylphenidate take to work
faqs.a: Most people start to feel the effect within 1 to 2 hours of a dose. The short acting form wears off after a few hours, while the long acting form is designed to last most of the day.

faqs.q: Can dexmethylphenidate stunt my child’s growth
faqs.a: Stimulants can reduce appetite and slow weight gain and sometimes height growth in children. The effect is usually small but can be important in some children. This is why height and weight are checked regularly. If growth slows too much, the prescriber may adjust the dose, switch medicines, or consider medication breaks when appropriate.

faqs.q: Why are extended release stimulants not recommended for children under 6
faqs.a: The FDA found that young children taking extended release stimulants had higher blood levels and more side effects, including significant weight loss of at least ten percent of body weight. Because of this, extended release products like Focalin XR are not recommended for children under 6.

Dexmethylphenidate has a high potential for abuse and addiction, which is why it is a Schedule II controlled substance. When used exactly as prescribed under medical supervision, the risk is lower, but misuse by taking higher doses, taking it more often than prescribed, or using it without a prescription can lead to addiction and serious health problems.

faqs.q: Can I drink coffee or energy drinks while on dexmethylphenidate
faqs.a: Small amounts of caffeine are usually acceptable, but high caffeine intake, such as energy drinks or many cups of coffee, can increase anxiety, racing heart, and trouble sleeping. It is best to limit caffeine and talk with your prescriber about what is reasonable for you.

Stopping dexmethylphenidate does not usually cause a classic withdrawal syndrome like some other medicine classes, but ADHD symptoms can return or feel worse for a time. Some people feel very tired or down when they stop suddenly. It is best to discuss a plan with your prescriber before stopping.

faqs.q: What should I do if my child is not eating well on Focalin or Focalin XR
faqs.a: Talk to the prescriber. Strategies include giving a good breakfast before the dose, offering high calorie snacks later in the day, and focusing on nutrient dense foods. If your child continues to lose weight or does not gain as expected, the dose or medication may need to be adjusted.

Yes. Dexmethylphenidate is used in adults with ADHD. It can improve focus, organization, and productivity. As with children, adults need monitoring for blood pressure, heart rate, mood, and possible misuse.
